title: About
text:
I am Karuna Reddy, an academic at the University of Auckland, where I work as a Professional Teaching Fellow in Data Science at the School of Computer Science, and also serve as Deputy Director of Data Science. I coordinate courses and supervise Masters and PhD students on research and industry projects.
My research is in survey sampling methodology, with a focus on optimal stratification, mathematical programming and optimisation, along with broader interests in data science and machine learning. I did my BSc, MSc and PhD at the University of the South Pacific (USP) in Fiji, and before Auckland, I was a Lecturer in Data Science at USP and also prior to that I was a Research Fellow in Survey Statistics at the Australian National University (ANU) in Canberra.
On this blog I share the R packages I build, such as stratifyR and FitVerse, with worked examples and notes on the methods behind them.

title: multistrata
text:
Multivariate Optimum Stratification and Sample Allocation
    
      
      
      
      
    
    
      install.packages("multistrata")  ·  library(multistrata)
stratifyR finds optimal boundaries for surveys stratified on a single variable. In practice, many surveys stratify on two or more variables at the same time and need to estimate several study variables well. multistrata extends stratifyR to that general case.
It jointly determines boundaries and sample allocation across multiple stratification variables and multiple study variables, minimising a weighted composite variance objective. The algorithm alternates between a boundary update and an exact generalised Neyman allocation, embedded in a multi-start scheme to avoid poor local solutions.

title: multistrata
text:
Quick Start
library(multistrata)

# simulate a two-variable population
set.seed(42)
pop <- sim_population(N = 5000, p = 2, q = 2, scenario = "independent")

# joint stratification on X1 and X2, estimating Y1 and Y2
res <- stratify_multi(
  data       = pop[, c("X1", "X2")],
  study_vars = pop[, c("Y1", "Y2")],
  H_vec      = c(3, 3),          # 3 strata per variable = 9 total strata
  n_total    = 500,
  omega      = c(0.5, 0.5),      # equal weight on both study variables
  n_starts   = 50
)
print(res)
summary(res)
H_vec gives the number of strata for each stratification variable. With H_vec = c(3, 3) you get a 3x3 grid of 9 strata in the joint space.

title: multistrata
text:
Core Function: stratify_multi()
The main function takes your population frame, your study variables, and a strata grid. It returns optimal boundaries, stratum sample sizes, and diagnostics.

Key arguments
stratify_multi(
  data,                    # stratification variables (N x p data frame or matrix)
  study_vars,              # study (target) variables (N x q)
  H_vec,                   # strata per variable, e.g. c(3, 3) or c(4, 2, 3)
  n_total,                 # total sample size
  omega      = NULL,       # study-variable weights (default: equal)
  constraint = "n_total",  # "n_total" or "cost"
  cost_total = NULL,       # budget C* (when constraint = "cost")
  cost_fixed = 0,          # fixed overhead deducted from budget
  cost_per_unit = 1,       # per-unit cost (scalar or H-vector)
  cv_targets = NULL,       # max CV per study variable, e.g. c(0.03, 0.03)
  distributions = NULL,    # NULL (empirical) or "auto" or named list of families
  method     = "cobyla",   # boundary solver: "cobyla" or "slsqp"
  n_starts   = 50,         # number of random starts
  n_min      = 2,          # minimum sample per stratum
  verbose    = FALSE,      # print per-start progress
  trace      = FALSE       # store per-iteration objective sequence
)






TipReproducibility



The multi-start scheme draws its initial boundaries at random. Always set a seed before any design you intend to report.
set.seed(1)
res <- stratify_multi(data, study_vars, H_vec = c(4, 3), n_total = 600)

title: multistrata
text:
Two Weight Modes
The stratum weights Wh (the fraction of the population in each stratum) can be estimated in two ways.

  
    Empirical mode (default)
    Wh is the sample proportion of units falling in each stratum. Uses only the data, no distributional assumptions. Set distributions = NULL.
  
  
    Parametric mode
    Wh is computed from marginal CDF differences under a fitted distribution. Set distributions = "auto" for AIC-based family selection, or supply families directly.
  

Auto mode picks the best-fitting marginal family per stratification variable:
res <- stratify_multi(
  data, study_vars, H_vec = c(3, 3), n_total = 500,
  distributions = "auto"
)
# res$.meta$distributions shows the selected families
You can also supply families directly:
dists <- list(
  X1 = list(family = "lnorm", meanlog = 1.2, sdlog = 0.8),
  X2 = list(family = "gamma", shape = 2.5, rate = 0.4)
)
res <- stratify_multi(data, study_vars, H_vec = c(3, 3), n_total = 500,
                      distributions = dists)
Supported families: norm, lnorm, gamma, exp, weibull, beta, unif, chisq, t, cauchy, logis, pareto, triang. When FitVerse is installed, auto mode can also search its 52 families.

title: multistrata
text:
Two Solvers

  
    COBYLA (default)
    method = "cobyla"Derivative-free constrained optimisation. Works in both empirical and parametric modes. Robust and fast for most problems.
  
  
    SLSQP
    method = "slsqp"Gradient-based solver using the closed-form weight gradient (Section 4.2 of the paper). Parametric mode only. Faster convergence when a good distribution fit is available.
  


Checking the solution
After fitting, check the quality diagnostics:
res$objective        # optimal composite variance Phi*
res$optimality_gap   # gap above the lower bound (0 = at the bound)
res$kkt_residual     # first-order stationarity residual
res$kkt_ok           # TRUE if residual is below tol_kkt
res$converged        # did the solver converge within max_iter?
res$n_starts_run     # number of random starts completed

title: multistrata
text:
Reading the Results
res$boundaries       # list of p boundary vectors (one per stratification variable)
res$allocation       # stratum sample sizes (integer vector of length H_total)
res$stratum_stats    # per-stratum N_h, W_h, n_h, A_h, within-stratum variances
The print method shows a formatted summary:
print(res)
================================================
  Multivariate Optimum Stratification (multistrata)
================================================
  Stratification variables : 2  (X1, X2)
  Study variables          : 2  (Y1, Y2)
  Strata per variable      : 3 x 3
  Total strata             : 9
  ...
  Composite variance (Phi) : 0.0048
  Optimality gap           : 0.12%
  Converged                : YES
  Multi-starts used        : 50

title: multistrata
text:
Precision-Driven Design: find_n()
The usual question is “given n, what is the best design?”. Sometimes the question runs the other way: “what is the smallest n that keeps all CVs below a target?”. find_n() answers that.
fn <- find_n(
  data       = pop[, c("X1", "X2")],
  study_vars = pop[, c("Y1", "Y2")],
  cv_targets = c(0.03, 0.03),     # max 3% CV on Y1 and Y2
  H_vec      = c(3, 3),
  n_starts   = 20
)
print(fn)
# fn$n          -- smallest feasible total sample size
# fn$allocation -- stratum sizes at that n
# fn$cv_achieved -- actual CVs achieved
It works by integer bisection over the CV-constrained allocation sub-problem. Boundaries are fixed from a single optimisation run and reused, which keeps the computation fast.

title: multistrata
text:
Choosing the Strata Grid: choose_H()
More strata always reduce variance, but the gains level off. choose_H() traces the optimal composite variance across a family of candidate grids and flags the elbow.
ch <- choose_H(
  data       = pop[, c("X1", "X2")],
  study_vars = pop[, c("Y1", "Y2")],
  n_total    = 500,
  H_each     = 2:5,       # tries 2x2, 3x3, 4x4, 5x5
  n_starts   = 10,
  plot       = TRUE
)
ch$table            # Phi*, optimality gap, relative gain per grid
ch$recommended      # recommended H_vec (elbow)
The plot shows the Phi* curve with the recommended grid marked. Go beyond the recommended grid only if the additional precision is worth the operational cost of more strata.

title: multistrata
text:
Priority Trade-Off: omega_sweep()
When you have two study variables and do not know how to weight them, omega_sweep() shows how the optimal design changes as the priority shifts from one to the other.
sw <- omega_sweep(
  data       = pop[, c("X1", "X2")],
  study_vars = pop[, c("Y1", "Y2")],
  H_vec      = c(3, 3),
  n_total    = 500,
  n_grid     = 11,           # 0%, 10%, ..., 100% weight on Y1
  n_starts   = 10
)
plot(sw)
The plot traces Phi* and per-variable variance against the weight on Y1. The flat middle region, if there is one, shows where the design is robust to the exact choice of weights.

title: multistrata
text:
Cost-Constrained Design
When sampling units in different strata cost different amounts, supply a per-stratum cost vector and a total budget instead of a fixed n.
res_cost <- stratify_multi(
  data          = pop[, c("X1", "X2")],
  study_vars    = pop[, c("Y1", "Y2")],
  H_vec         = c(3, 3),
  constraint    = "cost",
  cost_total    = 50000,
  cost_fixed    = 2000,         # fixed overhead (travel, setup)
  cost_per_unit = c(rep(20, 5), rep(40, 4)),   # H_total = 9 strata
  n_starts      = 30
)
The cost-aware design adjusts both boundaries and allocation. Strata with high per-unit costs get fewer units and the boundaries may shift to rebalance.

title: multistrata
text:
CV-Constrained Allocation
Specify maximum acceptable coefficients of variation for each study variable instead of (or alongside) a total sample size.
res_cv <- stratify_multi(
  data       = pop[, c("X1", "X2")],
  study_vars = pop[, c("Y1", "Y2")],
  H_vec      = c(3, 3),
  n_total    = 800,
  cv_targets = c(0.05, 0.04),   # 5% CV on Y1, 4% on Y2
  n_starts   = 30
)
res_cv$cv_achieved    # CVs actually achieved by the optimal allocation

title: multistrata
text:
Design Without Data: stratify_multi_density()
You can plan a stratified sample before collecting data, using assumed marginal distributions from a past survey or pilot study.
dists <- list(
  X1 = list(family = "lnorm", meanlog = 1.8, sdlog = 0.7),
  X2 = list(family = "gamma", shape = 3.0,   rate  = 0.5)
)
res_dens <- stratify_multi_density(
  distributions = dists,
  H_vec         = c(3, 3),
  n_total       = 400,
  omega         = c(0.5, 0.5)
)
Stratum weights are computed from the marginal CDFs. Study-variable moments come from Gauss-Kronrod quadrature of the marginal densities. This matches the empirical mode in the large-sample limit.

title: multistrata
text:
Survey Integration
Two functions take the optimal design into production.

assign_strata()
Applies the boundaries from a fitted design to any set of units: an estimation frame, a fresh census extract, or hold-out data.
# fit on a pilot sample, score the full frame
strata_labels <- assign_strata(res, newdata = full_frame[, c("X1", "X2")])
table(strata_labels)
The function matches columns by name when available, so you do not need to worry about column order.


as_svydesign()
Exports a survey::svydesign object ready for estimation with the survey package or srvyr.
svy <- as_svydesign(res, frame = pop)
# standard survey estimation from here
library(survey)
svymean(~Y1 + Y2, design = svy)

# or just a labelled frame for srvyr
labelled_frame <- as_svydesign(res, frame = pop, frame_only = TRUE)
# columns .stratum, .N_h, .n_h, .weight are added automatically

title: multistrata
text:
Visualisation

Boundary DiagramAllocation Bar ChartWeights Bar ChartOmega Sweep


plot_strata(res)
For one stratification variable: density with boundary walls. For two variables: a 3-D perspective plot of the joint density with boundary planes. The same function works for any number of variables.


plot(res, which = "allocation")
Bar chart of stratum sample sizes. Shows how the allocation spreads across strata.


plot(res, which = "weights")
Stratum weights Wh as a bar chart. Useful for checking how uniformly the population is distributed across strata.


sw <- omega_sweep(data, study_vars, H_vec = c(3, 3), n_total = 500)
plot(sw)
Traces the precision trade-off as the weight shifts between two study variables.

title: multistrata
text:
Benchmarking
benchmark_designs() compares the multistrata design against simpler alternatives: proportional allocation, equal allocation, and two classical boundary rules (Dalenius-Hodges and Gunning-Horgan).
bm <- benchmark_designs(res, pop)
print(bm)
Results show composite variance and per-variable CVs for each design at the same total sample size.

title: multistrata
text:
Simulated Populations
sim_population() generates test populations with known structures.
pop <- sim_population(N = 5000, p = 2, q = 2, scenario = "independent")
Available scenarios:







Scenario
Description




"independent"
Stratification and study variables uncorrelated


"correlated"
Moderate positive correlation between X and Y variables


"weibull_pareto"
Heavy-tailed establishment-survey archetype


"copula"
Dependent stratification variables via a Gaussian copula with log-normal margins

title: multistrata
text:
Shiny App
install.packages(c("shiny", "bslib", "DT", "plotly"))   # once
run_app()
The app exposes the full workflow without writing code:

Data input: upload your own CSV, generate a simulated population, or use one of the three built-in datasets
Design: set H_vec, n_total or budget, solver, weight mode, and omega
find_n: enter CV targets, get the minimum n
choose_H: scan candidate grids and view the elbow
Omega explorer: slide the priority weight and watch the design change
Benchmark: compare against proportional, equal, and classical rules
Visualise: boundary diagram, allocation bar chart, cost surface
Export: download report (PDF/HTML) and a reproducible R script with the set.seed() call

The generated R script includes the exact set.seed() call for the run shown on screen, so the design can be reproduced from the console.

title: multistrata
text:
Who Is multistrata For?

  🏛 National Statistical OfficesBusiness and agricultural surveys that stratify on size and sector simultaneously, with precision targets on multiple indicators.
  📐 Survey MethodologistsA reproducible, open implementation with formal convergence guarantees, optimality gaps, and KKT diagnostics for peer review.
  🔬 Applied ResearchersHealth, agricultural, economic, and environmental studies where more than one stratification variable is available at the design stage.
  📊 Planning-Stage DesignUse the density mode and find_n() to plan a complete survey before collecting data, from distributional assumptions alone.
  🎓 Teachers and StudentsThe Shiny app and sim_population() make the concepts of joint stratification and the Neyman trade-off easy to explore.

title: FitVerse
text:
Parametric Distribution Fitting in R
    
      
      
      
      
    
    
      install.packages("FitVerse")  ·  library(FitVerse)
Figuring out which distribution fits your data can take a while. Is it Gamma or Log-Normal? Maybe Weibull? Trying them one at a time is tedious, and eyeballing a histogram only gets you so far.
FitVerse does the searching for you. Give it your data and it fits all 52 distribution families, estimates parameters using MLE, MOM, or L-moments, ranks every fit, runs four goodness-of-fit tests, and returns a clean summary with plots. One line of code.

title: FitVerse
text:
Estimation Methods
MLE — Maximum Likelihood
MOM — Method of Moments
LMOM — L-Moments








Method
Best For
Notes




MLE
Most situations
Finds parameters that make observed data most probable


MOM
Quick estimates
Matches theoretical to sample moments; faster than MLE


LMOM
Hydrology; extreme values
Robust to outliers; ideal for flood peaks, rainfall maxima



Run all three at once with method = "ALL". FitVerse picks the overall best fit across all methods and distributions.

title: FitVerse
text:
Core Workflow

Quick Start
library(FitVerse)

# Built-in precip dataset: annual precipitation, 70 US cities
x <- as.numeric(precip)

# Fit all 52 distributions by MLE — ranked by AIC
fit <- fitverse(x, xlab = "Annual precipitation (inches)")






NoteWhat happens in one call



fitverse() fits all 52 distributions, estimates parameters, ranks by AIC, runs 4 GoF tests, and produces a two-panel diagnostic plot. It all happens automatically.




Key Arguments
fitverse(x,
  dists       = "all",    # subset: c("gamma","lognormal","gev") or "all"
  method      = "MLE",    # "MLE", "MOM", "LMOM", or "ALL"
  criterion   = "AIC",    # ranking criterion: "AIC" or "BIC"
  xlab        = "x",      # axis label for plots and reports
  plot        = TRUE,     # produce diagnostic plot?
  interactive = FALSE,    # plotly interactive? (needs plotly)
  top_n       = 3,        # density curves to overlay
  verbose     = TRUE)     # print ranked table to console?


The Return Object
fit$best_fit     # best-fit distribution: params, AIC/BIC, GoF stats
fit$ranking      # ranked table of all 52 distributions
fit$all_fits     # full list of every fitted model object
fit$data         # original data vector
fit$data_summary # n, mean, sd, skewness, kurtosis


S3 Methods

print(fit) — ranked table + best-fit parameters
summary(fit) — full goodness-of-fit table
plot(fit) — two-panel diagnostic plot
coef(fit) — best-fit parameter vector
logLik(fit)   AIC(fit)   BIC(fit)
nobs(fit) — sample size n
residuals(fit) — probability residuals
fitted(fit) — fitted densities at data points
confint(fit) — Wald confidence intervals for parameters
vcov(fit) — variance-covariance matrix
save_plot(fit, "fig.pdf", dpi = 600) — save plot to file

title: FitVerse
text:
Diagnostic Plot
Every call produces a two-panel diagnostic plot by default.
Left panel (Density): histogram with the top top_n fitted density curves overlaid. The best-fit distribution is highlighted and its PDF formula is shown on the figure.
Right panel (Q-Q plot): theoretical quantiles of the best-fit distribution plotted against sample quantiles. Points close to the diagonal mean a good fit.
# Interactive version (needs plotly)
fit <- fitverse(x, interactive = TRUE)

# Save without displaying
save_plot(fit, file = "precipitation_fit.png", dpi = 600)
save_plot(fit, file = "precipitation_fit.pdf")   # PDF or SVG by extension






TipL-Moment Ratio Diagram



For hydrological and extreme-value work, use the LMRD as an exploratory tool before fitting. It plots sample L-skewness and L-kurtosis against theoretical curves for several distribution families.
lmrd(x)

title: FitVerse
text:
Probability Tools
dfitverse(30,   fit)   # density (PDF) at x = 30
pfitverse(40,   fit)   # P(X ≤ 40)  — CDF
qfitverse(0.95, fit)   # 95th percentile
rfitverse(100,  fit)   # simulate 100 values from fitted distribution
Works identically for all 52 distributions — no need to know the underlying d/p/q/r function names.

title: FitVerse
text:
Bootstrap CIs & Return Levels

Parameter CIsReturn LevelsBootstrap CIs for Return Levels


boot <- bootstrap_ci(fit, R = 500)
print(boot)
# shape: [4.12, 6.10]   rate: [0.11, 0.17]


A T-year return level is the value expected to be exceeded once every T years on average.
rl <- return_level(fit, T = c(10, 50, 100))
print(rl)
# T =  10:  49.2  [43.1, 56.2]
# T =  50:  60.9  [53.4, 69.8]
# T = 100:  65.4  [57.0, 75.9]


boot_rl <- bootstrap_ci(fit, R = 500,
                        return_levels = c(10, 50, 100))
print(boot_rl)

Batch Fitting
results <- fitverse_batch(my_data, method = "MLE")
results$summary   # best distribution + parameters for each column
Fits all numeric columns of a data frame at once. Useful when you want a quick distributional overview across many variables.

  title       = "Precipitation Data: Distribution Fitting",

# Include bootstrap results

title: stratifyR 2.0-3
text:
Optimal Survey Stratification in R
    
      
      
      
      
    
    
      install.packages("stratifyR")  ·  library(stratifyR)
When your survey variable is continuous, like income, farm production, or claim size, you can cut its range into bands and sample from each band separately. The tricky part is deciding where the cuts should go, how many units to take from each band, and whether the precision gain is worth the effort.
stratifyR 2.0-3 works all of that out for you. One call gives you the optimal boundaries, the sample size per stratum, and a plain-language efficiency report.

title: stratifyR 2.0-3
text:
Quick Start
library(stratifyR)
data(sugarcane)   # 13,894 cane growers in Fiji

# 4 strata · total sample 500 · Dynamic Programming solver
res <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500, method = "dp")
summary(res)
One call fits the best distribution, finds optimal boundaries, and allocates the sample. The summary shows one row per stratum with the boundaries, weight, variance, and allocation.
res$OSB       # optimal stratum boundaries
res$nh        # sample sizes per stratum
res$Wh        # stratum weights
res$Vh        # within-stratum variances
res$WhSh      # each stratum's Neyman cost contribution
res$WhShTot   # total Neyman cost (lower = better)
res$distr     # fitted distribution name
res$fit       # fitted distribution parameters

title: stratifyR 2.0-3
text:
Distribution Fitting Step
Before placing any boundaries, strata.data() automatically fits your variable’s distribution from these candidates:
Normal · Log-Normal · Gamma · Weibull · Exponential · Cauchy · Uniform · Pareto · Triangular · Right-Triangular
The fitted distribution is used by the Dynamic Programming solver to compute each stratum’s contribution exactly. In 2.0-3 the Pareto and triangular fits work properly inside the package, and the Pareto likelihood is computed in a numerically stable form.






Tip



Already know the distribution? Use strata.distr() to supply it directly. No data needed (see Design Without Data).

title: stratifyR 2.0-3
text:
Four Solvers

  
    Dynamic Programming
    method = "dp"The default. Globally optimal on a fine grid for the fitted distribution, followed by a short local refinement that can only improve the answer.
  
  
    EXACT
    method = "exact"Dynamic programming on the data themselves. Returns the best possible partition of your sample. Exact for up to 20,000 distinct cut points.
  
  
    COBYLA
    method = "cobyla"Fast multi-start solver. One start comes from a quick coarse exact search, so it copes well with very skewed data. Best for interactive use.
  
  
    GLOBAL
    method = "global"Two phases: a broad DIRECT-L search on the rank scale, then a local refinement. A safe, fast choice for skewed data.
  

dp   <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500, method = "dp")
ex   <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500, method = "exact")
cob  <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500, method = "cobyla")
glob <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500, method = "global")

Solution Quality Diagnostics
For COBYLA and GLOBAL, check how close the solution is to optimal:
res$converged        # did the solver converge?
res$optimality_gap   # Cauchy-Schwarz gap: distance above the lower bound
res$kkt_residuals    # first-order optimality residuals

title: stratifyR 2.0-3
text:
Visualising the Design

2D Density Plot3D Cost SurfaceBoundary Explorer


Histogram with fitted density curve and colour-coded strata shading. Immediately shows where the boundaries fall and how the data mass is split.
plot(res)


Interactive plotly surface showing how the Neyman cost changes as boundaries move. Reveals that the optimum sits in a well.
plot(res, type = "3d")


One slider per interior boundary. Drag it and the Neyman cost updates in real time. Good for teaching and for checking how sensitive the design is to small boundary changes.
plot(res, type = "interactive")

title: stratifyR 2.0-3
text:
Design Efficiency Report
cd <- compare_designs(res)
cd
Compares three designs at the same sample size: Simple Random Sampling, Proportional Allocation, and Optimal Neyman Allocation. For each: variance, standard error, design effect, equivalent SRS size, and percentage saving.






NoteReading the report



The equivalent SRS size tells you how many units a simple random sample would need to match the precision of your stratified design. On skewed data such as the sugarcane production, it is many times larger than the stratified sample.

title: stratifyR 2.0-3
text:
Choosing the Number of Strata
More strata always lower the Neyman cost, but gains level off quickly. Scan a range and look for the elbow:
for (H in 2:6) {
  r <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = H, n = 500, method = "dp")
  cat("H =", H, "  Neyman cost =", round(r$WhShTot, 2), "\n")
}
The Shiny app does this automatically and marks the recommended stratum count on the curve.

title: stratifyR 2.0-3
text:
Design Without Data
You can plan the full design before any fieldwork using an assumed distribution from a past round or pilot study:
# Household income survey: log-normal, 20,000 units, n = 1,000
g <- strata.distr(h = 4, initval = 500, dist = 119500,
                  distr = "lnorm",
                  params = c(meanlog = 9.616, sdlog = 0.703),
                  n = 1000, N = 20000, method = "dp")
summary(g)
compare_designs(g)

title: stratifyR 2.0-3
text:
Cost-Constrained Allocation
When sampling costs differ by stratum (large units cost more to visit):
ch <- c(20, 30, 50, 80)   # cost per sampled unit, stratum 1 to 4

cost_res <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500,
                        method = "dp", cost = TRUE, ch = ch)
The cost-aware design adjusts both the boundaries and the allocation, and moves more of the sample into the cheaper strata, so the same total n costs less in the field. Its variance is a little higher than the Neyman design’s, so it is the better choice when the budget, rather than the sample size, is fixed.

title: stratifyR 2.0-3
text:
Shiny App
install.packages(c("shiny", "bslib", "DT"))   # once
stratifyRApp()
The app covers the full workflow across eight tabs:

Optimal Boundaries: per-stratum summary table + 2D density plot
Design Comparison: variance, SE, design effect vs. SRS and proportional
Strata Count: Neyman cost curve with elbow recommendation
Boundary Methods: DP vs. classical boundary rules side by side
Sample Size: target precision to required sample size
Allocation: SRS / proportional / Neyman compared
Cost-Constrained: enter per-stratum costs and see the cost-aware design
Visualise: 2D density, 3D cost surface, interactive boundary explorer

title: stratifyR 2.0-3
text:
What Is New in Version 2.0-3
Versions 2.0-2 and 2.0-3 are accuracy releases. They came out of a large simulation study (ten distributions, 20 random seeds, two to six strata), checked against the exact optimum.
NEWExact solver: method = "exact" runs dynamic programming on the data and returns the best possible partition. It is also the reference the other solvers are checked against.
BETTERCOBYLA and GLOBAL now reach the exact optimum, or come within about 0.1% of it, on every population in the study, including very heavy-tailed ones such as Pareto and Cauchy samples.
BETTERDP adds a short local refinement after the grid search, and two traceback fixes make it more robust on heavy-tailed data.
FIXDistribution fitting: Pareto and triangular fits now work inside the package, with a numerically stable Pareto likelihood and robust Cauchy starting values.
FIXBoundaries and costs: boundaries are kept at full precision, every unit is always counted, and tied values are never split across strata.
FIXstrata.distr() now gives stratum sizes that add up to N exactly, and gives a clear message when the range lies outside a uniform or triangular distribution.
COMPATFully backward-compatible. Existing strata.data() and strata.distr() calls work unchanged.
Already in 2.0: the COBYLA and GLOBAL solvers, cost-constrained allocation, compare_designs(), solution-quality diagnostics, the 2D, 3D and interactive plots, and the Shiny app.

title: stratifyR 2.0-3
text:
Who Is stratifyR For?

  Statistical OfficesBusiness, agricultural, and household surveys where good stratification cuts the sample size (and cost) needed to hit a target precision.
  Survey MethodologistsAn open, reproducible implementation with a globally optimal solver to benchmark against classical boundary rules.
  Applied ResearchersHealth, economics, agriculture, environment. Design an efficient sample at the planning stage using an assumed distribution.
  Teachers & StudentsThe app and interactive plots show how boundaries and allocation affect an estimate, with no code needed.

title: clusta
text:
Spectral, Distribution-Aware and Dynamic-Programming Clustering
    
      
      
      
      
    
    
      install.packages("clusta")  ·  library(clusta)
Most clustering methods fail on non-convex shapes. Two interleaved crescents, concentric rings, or three spirals will confuse k-means because it partitions space with straight cuts. clusta is built around S-MPDP (Spectral Mathematical Programming Dynamic Programming), a method that first unfolds the data into a one-dimensional signal using a spectral graph, then finds cluster boundaries on that signal with an exact dynamic program.
Beyond S-MPDP, clusta also provides globally optimal one-dimensional clustering, exact solutions for two-variable problems, projection-based methods for higher dimensions, and sequence or graph-constrained clustering. One consistent interface covers all of them.

title: clusta
text:
Quick Start
library(clusta)

# one variable: globally optimal partition
x  <- c(rnorm(60, 0), rnorm(60, 6), rnorm(60, 13))
cl <- clusta(x, k = 3)
print(cl)
plot(cl)

# two moons: non-convex, use S-MPDP
d  <- gen_two_moons()
cl <- clusta(d[, c("x", "y")], k = 2, method = "spectral")
plot(cl)

# iris: multivariate, project to PC1 then exact DP
cl <- clusta(iris[, 1:4], k = 3, method = "projection")

title: clusta
text:
Nine Clustering Methods
clusta picks a sensible default based on the data (one variable gives "wcss", multiple variables give "projection"), or you can set method explicitly.

  
    1D EXACT
    wcss
    Globally optimal contiguous partition of one variable by minimising within-cluster sum of squares. Returns a certified gap of 0%.
  
  
    MULTIVARIATE
    projection
    Projects to the first principal component (or a custom direction) then runs the exact 1-D DP on the score. Exact on the projection axis.
  
  
    MULTIVARIATE
    estvar
    Exact DP using an estimation-variance criterion. The Neyman objective (sum of Wh*Sh) is globally optimal. Also supports Gaussian and WCSS objectives.
  
  
    DISTRIBUTION
    parametric
    Fits the best parametric distribution by AIC, then places boundaries with a DP on the model's Wh*Sh cost. Optionally uses FitVerse for 52 families.
  
  
    FLAGSHIP
    spectral
    S-MPDP. Builds a k-NN graph, unfolds the data to a 1-D signal via the normalised Laplacian, then runs the distribution-fitting DP. Handles non-convex shapes.
  
  
    2D EXACT
    exact2d
    Exactly two variables, k = 2. Enumerates all separating directions and returns the certified global optimum in full 2-D space.
  
  
    2D
    sweep
    Two variables, any k. Global for k = 2; best clustering separable by parallel lines for k >= 3. Report the optimality gap to assess quality.
  
  
    SEQUENTIAL
    sequence
    Ordered data (time series, spatial transects, trajectories). Exact multivariate segment DP along the given order.
  
  
    SPATIAL
    graph
    Contiguity-constrained clustering on a neighbourhood graph using minimum spanning tree and greedy edge removal. Respects spatial adjacency.

title: clusta
text:
S-MPDP: The Flagship Method
Standard spectral clustering runs k-means on the eigenvectors of a graph Laplacian. S-MPDP replaces that k-means step with a dynamic program, which means it finds boundaries on the spectral signal exactly rather than approximately.
The algorithm has two stages. Stage 1 builds a mutual k-nearest-neighbour graph and computes the normalised Laplacian. The leading eigenvectors unfold the local neighbourhood structure into a one-dimensional score. Stage 2 fits the best parametric distribution to that score by AIC and places boundaries with an exact DP. The distribution fitting step lets the DP account for the shape of the signal rather than treating it as uniform.
# dedicated interface with full control
cl <- spectral_mpdp(d[, c("x", "y")], k = 2, k_neighbors = 15)

# or through clusta()
cl <- clusta(d[, c("x", "y")], k = 2, method = "spectral", k_neighbors = 15)






NoteFitVerse integration



Set fit_engine = "fitverse" in method = "parametric" to search all 52 distribution families rather than the default five. Set fit_engine = "best" to run both engines and keep whichever gives lower empirical Wh*Sh.
cl <- clusta(x, k = 3, method = "parametric", fit_engine = "fitverse")

title: clusta
text:
Choosing k

Eigengap method
The Stage 1 graph is already built during clustering, so reading its Laplacian spectrum is cheap. A clear gap between consecutive eigenvalues points at the number of clusters in the data.
sk <- suggest_k(d[, c("x", "y")], k_neighbors = 15, k_max = 8)
sk          # prints the suggested k and the gap sizes
plot(sk)    # eigenvalue spectrum with gap highlighted


Elbow scan
clusta_elbow() runs clusta() for a range of k values and plots WCSS, BIC, and silhouette side by side.
x <- c(rnorm(80, 0), rnorm(80, 6), rnorm(80, 13))
clusta_elbow(x, k_range = 1:8)
Both are second opinions. A clear isolated gap from suggest_k() and an elbow from clusta_elbow() agreeing on the same k is a good sign.

title: clusta
text:
Bootstrap Stability
After clustering, cluster_stability() checks whether the clusters would reappear in a fresh sample. It resamples the data with replacement, re-runs the full S-MPDP pipeline on each resample, and measures the Jaccard overlap between original and resample clusters.
stab <- cluster_stability(d[, c("x", "y")], h = 2,
                          k_neighbors = 15, B = 50, seed = 42)
print(stab)
plot(stab)
A common reading of the per-cluster mean Jaccard score:
above 0.85 — highly stable
0.75 to 0.85 — stable
0.60 to 0.75 — doubtful
below 0.60 — likely an artefact
Treat a cluster scoring below 0.60 as a feature of this particular sample rather than a real structure in the population.

title: clusta
text:
Sensitivity Analysis
smpdp_sensitivity() evaluates combinations of neighbourhood size and cluster count, reporting quality metrics for each combination. Useful when you are unsure about k_neighbors.
sens <- smpdp_sensitivity(d[, c("x", "y")],
                          k_vec     = 2:4,
                          kn_vec    = c(10, 15, 20, 30),
                          B_stab    = 10)
print(sens)
plot(sens)

title: clusta
text:
Evaluation Metrics
cluster_metrics() computes a comprehensive set of internal and external validity scores for any clustering result.
data(ceramic)
X  <- ceramic[, setdiff(names(ceramic), "class")]
cl <- clusta(X, k = 3, method = "spectral", k_neighbors = 41)
cluster_metrics(cl, true_labels = ceramic$class)







Metric
What it measures




ARI
Agreement with ground-truth labels (adjusted for chance)


NMI
Normalised mutual information with ground-truth labels


Silhouette
Cohesion vs separation without ground truth


Purity
Majority-class proportion per cluster


Calinski-Harabasz
Between-to-within variance ratio


Davies-Bouldin
Average ratio of within-to-between spread


Dunn
Minimum inter-cluster distance / maximum intra-cluster diameter

title: clusta
text:
Benchmarking
run_clustering_benchmarks() compares S-MPDP against k-means, spectral clustering (from the cluster package), HDBSCAN, and agglomerative clustering across several datasets.
bm <- run_clustering_benchmarks(datasets = "all", metrics = "all")
print(bm)
friedman_ranks() summarises the comparison with Friedman rank scores, one row per method, one column per metric.

title: clusta
text:
Bundled Datasets
Six real datasets are bundled with the package. Each has numeric feature columns and a class factor for validation.

  glass214 glass fragments, 9 oxide predictors, 6 glass types.
  breast_cancer569 tumour measurements, 30 features, benign vs malignant.
  raisin900 raisin samples, 7 morphological features, 2 varieties.
  rice3810 rice samples, 7 shape features, 2 varieties.
  ceramic88 ceramic fragments, chemical composition, archaeological classification.
  smpdp_toySmall synthetic dataset for quick demos and testing.

Six synthetic shape generators are also included for experimenting with non-convex structures.

Two MoonsConcentric CirclesThree SpiralsSmileyV-ShapeCassini


d <- gen_two_moons(n = 500)
cl <- clusta(d[, c("x","y")], k = 2, method = "spectral")
plot(cl)
Two interleaved crescent shapes. k-means fails; S-MPDP finds the correct boundary.


d <- gen_concentric_circles(n = 2000)
cl <- clusta(d[, c("x","y")], k = 2, method = "spectral")
plot(cl)
Inner and outer rings. A textbook failure case for any linear or convex method.


d <- gen_three_spirals(n = 1200, cycles = 1.4)
cl <- clusta(d[, c("x","y")], k = 3, method = "spectral")
plot(cl)
Three interleaved arms. Tests the graph unfolding under high curvature.


d <- gen_smiley(n = 400)
cl <- clusta(d[, c("x","y")], k = 3, method = "spectral")
plot(cl)
A smile arc and two eyes. Three clusters with very different densities.


d <- gen_v_shape(n = 400)
cl <- clusta(d[, c("x","y")], k = 2, method = "spectral")
plot(cl)
Two arms of a V. Non-convex but less extreme than spirals.


d <- gen_cassini(n = 2000)
cl <- clusta(d[, c("x","y")], k = 3, method = "spectral")
plot(cl)
Two outer banana-shaped bands and a central disc. Uses the mlbench generator when installed.

title: clusta
text:
Visualisation

Cluster PlotSignal PlotConfidence PlotEigengap PlotSimilarity Matrix


plot(cl)                  # base graphics
fviz_clusta(cl)           # ggplot2 version
Scatter plot coloured by cluster assignment. For one-variable results, shows the density with boundaries marked.


plot(cl, type = "signal")
The 1-D spectral signal used by S-MPDP, with fitted density and cluster boundaries overlaid.


plot(cl, type = "confidence")
Per-observation assignment confidence, based on distance to the nearest boundary in signal space.


sk <- suggest_k(X)
plot(sk)
Laplacian eigenvalue spectrum with the largest gap highlighted.


plot(cl, type = "similarity")
The kNN similarity matrix, reordered by cluster. Block structure confirms cluster quality.

title: clusta
text:
S3 Methods

print(cl)   cluster sizes, centres, WCSS, BIC, silhouette, optimality gap
summary(cl)   per-cluster table with size, proportion, within-SS, silhouette width
plot(cl)   cluster plot (base graphics)
autoplot(cl)   cluster plot (ggplot2)
fitted(cl)   centre coordinates for each observation
predict(cl, newdata)   assign new points to the nearest cluster centre
fviz_clusta(cl)   ggplot2 visualisation with confidence shading


Optimality Gap
For the exact one-dimensional methods and exact2d, clusta certifies how close the solution is to the global optimum.
cl$gap_pct        # certified upper bound on distance from global (0 = provably global)
cl$lower_bound    # Cauchy-Schwarz lower bound on WCSS
A gap of 0% means the solution is certifiably the best possible. For spectral and parametric methods the objective is not WCSS, so the gap is not reported.

title: clusta
text:
Shiny App
install.packages(c("shiny", "bslib", "DT", "ggplot2"))   # once
clustaApp()
The bundled app covers the full workflow: upload data or pick a built-in dataset, choose the method and k, view cluster plots, signal plots, eigengap, stability results, and a benchmark comparison. No code needed.

title: clusta
text:
Who Is clusta For?

  🔬 Applied ResearchersAny domain with non-convex or ring-like cluster structures. The spectral method works where k-means does not.
  📊 Survey and Social ScienceThe estvar method with the Neyman objective clusters in a way that directly minimises survey estimation variance.
  🌍 Spatial AnalysisThe graph method respects spatial adjacency constraints, so neighbouring units stay in the same cluster.
  📈 Time SeriesThe sequence method segments ordered data into contiguous groups along a known ordering.
  🎓 TeachingThe Shiny app and shape generators make it easy to show students why k-means fails on non-convex data.
